newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamists buy time in army dispute.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamists buy time in army dispute.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has bought his government time with concessions to the secularist army in a dispute over the role of Islam in public life.
The Turkish press on Sunday said Erbakan, the NATO member country's first Islamist leader in modern times, had bowed to a key demand by the military to ask MPs to expand secularist education.
But Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party, afraid of losing grassroot support, will attempt to oppose the education changes in parliament.

"Erbakan has agreed to eight years of basic education," the Radikal daily quoted Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller as saying after a marathon meeting of the army-dominated National Security Council on Saturday.

The planned education reform, under which children would receive eight years of compulsory secularist education from the current five, is one of the generals' key demands for a reversal of an Islamist upsurge encouraged by Welfare.
Two conservative ministers from Ciller's wing of the ruling alliance resigned at the weekend in frustration at Erbakan's attempts to stall the influential army.
The ministers hinted others would step down soon.
Erbakan on Saturday signed a security council communique that urges the cabinet to instigate the anti-Islamist crackdown.
"This is the modern Turkish republic....Nobody should pay any attention to those who are trying to make this issue out to be a problem," the Sabah daily quoted Erbakan as telling the generals.

A senior Islamist, however, said Welfare could not pass the secularist education draft when it came to parliament. "As a party close to the people, Welfare will do all it can to oppose such a motion," deputy Salih Kapusuz told a news conference.
A feud between Welfare and the army reached a peak last week when the Islamists threatened legal action against a general who called Erbakan a "pimp".
The army has ousted three governments since 1960 but is reluctant to stage another coup for fear of damaging Turkey's prized ties to Europe and the United States.
Some of Erbakan's younger aides have urged him to break the coalition and try to appeal to voters as a defender of democracy who was forced out of office by the army.
But general elections are not due until the year 2000 and MPs, who would lose wide-ranging privileges if parliament were dissolved, are reluctant to go to snap polls.

Political analysts say many deputies from Ciller's party could be enticed by the opposition into rebelling against the government in the hope of forming an alliance to govern with other secularist parties.
Secularist disunity allowed the Islamists into power last year after Welfare had narrowly won the last general polls, in December 1995, with 21 percent of the vote.
